newsitem.title: USA: Lake says CIA must probe "hard targets" deeper.
newsitem.headline: Lake says CIA must probe "hard targets" deeper.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice to be the next CIA chief said on Wednesday that U.S. intelligence agencies should do a better job at investigating countries that Washington alleges sponsor acts of terror.

"We need to do a better job than we have done in the past in cracking 'hard targets' like North Korea and Cuba and Iraq and Iran and the others because that is where the support for many of these theats is coming from," Anthony Lake said on the second day of his Senate confirmation hearings.
Syria, Libya and Sudan are the other countries the United States accuses of involvement in state-supported terrorism.
Lake told the Select Committee on Intelligence that U.S. spy agencies also must go further to be able to "pick off" small-scale chemical and biological warfare programmes.
"I think we have a lot more to do. We need all the tools we can get to attack those targets. We're not there yet," he said in reply to Sen. John Glenn, an Ohio Democrat.
Lake said he would like to reward Central Intelligence Agency personnel who tackle tough jobs even if they fail.

"Even if they fail at hard things, if they did it right and they did it honestly they need to be rewarded for it," he said. "It doesn't help us or the national interest very much when they do easy things."

Lake, Clinton's first-term national security adviser, applied this formula to clandestine operatives who recruit spies abroad as well as to their desk-bound colleagues "when they make tough analytical calls."

He endorsed the CIA's recent purge of foreign informants judged to be outdated or whose value as tipsters was outweighed by the stigma of shady or criminal pasts. He said the worldwide "agent scrub," as it was known inside the CIA, had been completed. It took place mainly under CIA Director John Deutch, who left in December after 20 months in office.
New CIA recruitment curbs have sparked controversy among those who fear they may hinder U.S. ability to infiltrate terrorist cells, drug gangs and other criminal enterprises.

But Lake, who has spent much time in recent months at CIA headquarters schooling himself in the job, rejected the notion that the shedding of links to the worst offenders would lead to "risk aversion" among field officers.

Much of the hearing's anticipated political tension evaporated by day two, strengthening the prospect that the 19-member intelligence panel will approve the nomination, which could still run into problems in the full Senate. Hearings were to continue on Thursday behind closed doors to discuss classified matters, with three more sessions next week, at least two of them in public.

Committee Chairman Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican who said he was troubled by Lake's management decisions, returned for a second day to Lake's handling of the National Security Council staff last June, when the FBI briefed two aides on an alleged Chinese plan to influence U.S. elections.

Lake reiterated that he should have been alerted about the FBI's concerns over any Chinese plan to steer funds secretly to candidates for federal office. "There appears to have been some kind of a breakdown here," he said of the failure to pass the alert up the line to him.

But he denied it was indicative of any systematic failure of his own to properly manage the 151-member council staff. If confirmed, Lake would run the CIA and preside over its 12 companion executive branch espionage outfits, which together account for about $30 billion a year in U.S. spending and employ tens of thousands of people.
